title: Broadcasting and Other Legislation Amendment (Deregulation) Bill 2015
short_title: Broadcasting and Other Legislation Amendment (Deregulation) Bill 2015

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would cut red tape for broadcasters by removing outdated rules and simplifying processes.
It would change the Broadcasting Services Act 1992, the Radiocommunications Act 1992 and the Australian Communications and Media Authority Act 2005.
The explanatory memorandum says the bill would repeal rules for the digital switchover, streamline spectrum planning, and relax captioning and audit requirements.
changes: Repeal redundant licensing and planning provisions for the digital switchover and restack.
Amend ACMA's planning powers to make spectrum planning more efficient.
Give free-to-air and subscription TV broadcasters more flexibility in meeting captioning obligations.
Remove the requirement for independent audits of reports under the New Eligible Drama Expenditure Scheme.
Make minor amendments to control and ownership provisions.
Remove the requirement for ACMA to periodically review certain industry code matters.
summary.affected: The broadcasting industry, including free-to-air and subscription television broadcasters, and the Australian Communications and Media Authority.

divisions.question: Stephen Conroy I rise to speak on the Broadcasting and Other Legislation Amendment (Deregulation) Bill 2015. Labor supports this bill. This bill is part of the government's so-called regulation repeal day. This is another government stunt designed to do little more than simply generate a news headline. The former Labor government repealed 16,974 acts and regulations during its time in office. Let me repeat that: the former Labor government repealed 16,974 acts and regulations during its time in office. We called this 'governing'. This bill saves industry about $350,000 according to estimates from the Department of Communications. Important—yes. But hardly worth a special day. The last time I spoke in this place on red tape repeal it was to amend the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill 2014. The Senate agreed to this amendment which would ensure a proper process for Australia's Future Submarine project. Given what has happened in the recent past on this issue, since this amendment was passed, it shows how vital this amendment was; it languishes in the other place, sitting at the bottom of the _Notice Paper_. It is another indication that the Prime Minister is still committed to his captain's pick on Japanese submarines. On the bill before the Senate now, Labor does not propose any amendments. But I do have to note, particularly as there are some South Australians in the chamber today, that this morning in _The Australian_ the government finally admitted that, yes, they did draw up press releases to announce the Japanese had won the submarine contract and they were going to announce it at G20. So despite all of the fabrications that have taken place over the last six months, there is a little paragraph at the end that said: look we might have done a deal with the Japanese before but trust us we have got a proper process in place now. speeches.speaker: Jason Clare
speeches.brief: Said this regulation repeal day bill will save industry only $350,000, far less than the $35 million saved by the government's first repeal bill, and announced Labor amendments, agreed to by the government, restoring annual captioning compliance reporting and a 2016 statutory review after Deaf Australia said it was not properly consulted.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Defended the broadcasting deregulation bill as reducing an excessive regulatory burden, noting Australia ranked 124th of 148 countries for regulation and that compliance costs could reach 4 per cent of GDP, and said the communications portfolio's red tape cuts have already saved over $70 million and repealed 3,400 pages of regulation.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Rowland
speeches.brief: Detailed Labor's captioning amendments to the broadcasting deregulation bill, quoting a Senate committee finding that consultation with Deaf Australia and other accessibility groups had been inadequate, and highlighted a lack of audio description for Australia's 600,000 blind and vision-impaired people following the closure of the ABC's Ramp Up disability website.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Detailed ongoing poor digital television reception across the Paterson electorate since analog switch-off in November 2012, blamed frequency clashes between the Newcastle and Illawarra transmitters, and called on Regional Broadcasting Australia to urgently submit its proposal for new transmitter towers.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Said constituents in central Victoria are more concerned about slow broadband than television reception, noted the broadcasting deregulation bill will save industry only about $350,000, and lamented that this will be the last WNBL season broadcast on the ABC after a 35-year partnership.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Opposed the suspension of standing orders, arguing the government is focused on jobs, growth and family issues, citing 600 new jobs a day and 2.7 per cent growth compared with 1.9 per cent under the previous government, and accused the Leader of the Opposition of hypocrisy for having played a role in removing two prime ministers.

speeches.speaker: Nick Champion
speeches.brief: Supported the broadcasting deregulation bill, noted the previous Labor government had already repealed 16,794 acts and regulations without fanfare, and described how the suburbs of Hillbank and Craigmore endured 25 years of poor television reception because they sat in the shadow of the Mount Lofty television tower.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: Supported the broadcasting deregulation bill, said government revenue is $110 million a day short of expenditure, reported his electorate nominated more than 140 mobile phone black spot sites, and recounted how constituent Derek Thompson of Moltema lost television reception entirely during the digital switchover.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Supported the amended broadcasting deregulation bill, noting that one in six Australians are affected by hearing loss and around 30,000 have total hearing loss, and welcomed Labor's amendments restoring a statutory review of captioning obligations to take place in 2016.

speeches.speaker: Brett Whiteley
speeches.brief: Argued that opposition members were scaremongering by suggesting the broadcasting deregulation bill would harm people with a hearing impairment, saying they use the same tactics used to try to scare students and pensioners.

speeches.speaker: Jenny Macklin
speeches.brief: Supported Labor's amendments to restore annual captioning compliance reporting and a statutory review in 2016, criticised the government for cutting funding to Deaf Australia and the Deafness Forum of Australia, which together represent about four million deaf or hard of hearing Australians, and congratulated Drisana Levitzke-Gray on being named Young Australian of the Year for her advocacy for deaf children.

speeches.speaker: Keith Pitt
speeches.brief: Supported the broadcasting deregulation bill, recalled buying a 386SX computer for about $2,500 to illustrate how fast technology has changed, and praised ABC regional radio staff for their emergency broadcasts during the Rockhampton and Yeppoon natural disasters, noting the region's NBN network has only about eight hours of backup power during outages.

speeches.speaker: Malcolm Turnbull
speeches.brief: Reported on the government's consultation timeline for the broadcasting deregulation bill, including a 15 May meeting with the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network, his own 31 October meeting with the Human Rights Commission, and a 21 November meeting between his staff and Deaf Australia and other advocacy groups, and agreed to accept Labor's amendments to the bill.
